learn.title: Giving memory back
learn.body: `free(p)` returns a block to the heap so it can be reused. Pass it exactly the pointer that `malloc` gave you. The rule is one `free` for every successful `malloc`. Forgetting leaks memory, and freeing twice is a bug.

learn.title: Copying a string
learn.body: This prints `memory Memory`. We need `strlen + 1` bytes: the extra byte is for the ending 0. After `free`, `copy` still holds the old address, so we set it to `NULL`.

learn.title: Dangling pointers
learn.body: After `free(p)`, the variable `p` still holds the old address, but the memory is no longer yours. Using it is a bug. Setting `p = NULL;` right after is a cheap safety habit, and `free(NULL)` does nothing, so it is always safe.

learn.title: Counting the bytes for a copy
learn.body: How much space does a copy of `"memory"` need?
Whoever allocates should decide who frees. Write that down in a comment when a function hands a heap pointer to its caller.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does a copy of `"memory"` need?
questions.explanation: Six letters plus the ending 0 byte.
It still holds the old address, but that memory is no longer yours.

questions.prompt: What is a good habit right after `free(p)`?
questions.explanation: A null pointer is easy to test and harmless to free.

questions.prompt: How many `free` calls does one successful `malloc` need?
questions.explanation: One free per malloc: not zero (leak), not two (double free).

questions.prompt: Why is `malloc(strlen(src))` too small for a copy?
choices: It leaves no room for the ending 0
questions.explanation: `strlen` does not count the 0 byte that ends the string.

questions.prompt: Put these in the safest order.
questions.explanation: Freeing then clearing the pointer prevents accidental reuse.
